newsitem.title: UK: Euro stocks drift lower as Wall St holidays.
newsitem.headline: Euro stocks drift lower as Wall St holidays.

text.p: European stock markets drifted lower on Monday as a Wall Street holiday cleared the stage for investors to take profits from a long bull run.
The foreign exchange market also lacked inspiration due to the President's Day holiday in the United States.

The dollar was firm against a mark undermined by more European monetary union worries, although it slipped from Asian highs against the yen as unease grew that the Bank of Japan might intervene on markets.
British, German and French stocks were all lower following a weaker Friday close on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones Industrial average ended down 33.48 points at 6,988.96..
"Wall Street has been one of the main things driving us along and that's closed today," one London trader said. "We're unlikely to want to go too much higher on our own."
Deprived of action, dealers began to wonder how long the New Year bull run, inspired by Wall Street, could last.
"Some people are trying to call the top (of the market)," one said. "With the Dow going above 7,000 and then closing below it, some people there are a little more pessimistic."
In London, the FTSE 100 index was down 11.7 points at 4,329.3 at mid-afternoon after closing at a record on Friday.

Investors suffered the additional worries of a strong pound, which hurts British exporters, and a parliamentary vote scheduled for Monday night which is aimed at bringing down the Conservative government. "Nobody likes this kind of instability," one dealer said.

The opposition Labour Party will try to bring down the government with a vote expected around 2200 GMT on whether to censure Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg over his handling of the mad cow disease crisis.
If Prime Minister John Major lost, there could be a confidence vote in the government the next day. If he lost that vote, Major would have call an early general election.
However, Monday's vote was little more than a nagging worry as Major is expected to win it narrowly and he has to call an election by May in any case.

German stocks likewise fell, with dealers citing profit-taking after 11 consecutive record closes plus Friday's losses on Wall Street. The DAX index closed down 15.61 points at 3,232.57 and German dealers welcomed the drop.
"Everyone here is hoping that the market will fall back so that taking new positions will be cheaper. After 11 record days, a breathing space will do nothing but good," said one.

Profit-takers pushed down the Paris market in the morning but by mid-afternoon the CAC 40 index was down just 1.08 at 2,626.34. Car maker Renault tumbled 3.43 percent after warning last week that its losses would be worse than the market expected.

On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar was buoyant against the mark and Swiss franc but below overnight highs against the yen, weakened by a Tokyo report that Japan would intervene alone if the yen fell sharply.
Uncertainty over whether the single European currency, the euro, would be launched on schedule in 1999 hurt the mark.

German unemployment at the highest level since the 1930s has cast doubt on whether Bonn can meet a target for cutting its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, a key criterion for monetary union membership.
The German State Secretary for Finance Juergen Stark insisted on Monday that the target would be met. But not everyone on the financial markets believes him.

"There's a risk premium related to the uncertainty on what's going to happen to the mark and what kind of euro we'll have and when, and until this issue is clarified it will almost always be negative for the deutschemark," said Giorgio Radaelli, senior international economist at Lehman Brothers in London.

The dollar was at 1.6950 marks, up from Friday's 1.6878 close but off the overnight 34-month high of 1.6962, while it was stuck at 124.22 yen, little changed from its previous finish in Europe and below its Asian high of 124.67.

With the dollar surging against the yen, Jiji news agency said the United States had agreed at the recent meeting of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations to unilateral Japanese action on the foreign exchange market.
This would mark an abandoning of old U.S. objections due to fears of a growing Japanese current account surplus and complaints from U.S. industry over the dollar's strength.

Again, the U.S. holiday subdued foreign exchange trade but analysts said thin volume could mean choppy conditions. Some argued that this might tempt central banks to launch a round of intervention. But the dollar could soon push ahead again.

"If the market feels it's only odd people within G7 who want this to stop, or they feel they're only going to have a tickle with it, I think the market will take the dollar higher," said Graham Cocks, vice-president, treasury at Bank of Boston in London.
CURRENCIES at 1530 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.6950 marks and 124.22 yen compared with 1.6878 marks and 124.67 yen in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS at 1530 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 11.7 points at 4,329.3.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was 1.08 lower at 2,626.34 points.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed 15.61 points lower at 3,232.57.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $344.10 an ounce in the afternoon, compared with Friday's close of $343.05. Silver was at $5.21, up five cents from Friday's close.
